challenges.prompt:
# Prompt for coin-select

You are working on the research challenge `coin-select`: Cardano UTxO coin selection
(CIP-2). Read `contracts/wallet/INTERFACE.md` and `contracts/wallet/CHOICES.md`, then
`DIRECTIONS.md` (what has been tried, what is open and the cheapest test for each
open idea), `submissions/` and `taxonomy.toml`. The baseline is a Python largest-first.

Create ONE new directory `submissions/<id>/` and change nothing else. It needs a
`submission.toml`, an executable `build.sh` that leaves an executable `./select`, and
your code; see `SUBMITTING.md` for the fields. Either start a new direction (random
improve, branch and bound, consolidation policies, ...) or copy an accepted
submission's directory and build on it. Declare novelty honestly: porting an accepted
submission to another language, or retuning its constants or seed, is `builds-on`,
not a new direction. You choose which axes in `challenge.toml` to push (fees, dust,
inputs per transaction, latency, memory): they are measured, recorded and never
ranked or combined, so a trade-off is a fine result. Run the judge locally (see
`README.md`) before opening a PR.

submissions.readme: The reference submission for wallet@1: Python largest-first. It sorts the wallet by value, adds inputs until they cover the outputs and the fee (priced with one change output), makes a single change output when the leftover is at least min-ada, and otherwise folds the leftover into the fee. It refuses only when the whole wallet cannot pay. It is the root of the lineage tree and the yardstick for preflight.
submissions.summary: CIP-2 largest-first: take the biggest UTxOs until the payment and fee are covered, one change output.

submissions.readme: CIP-2 Random-Improve in std-only Rust. UTxOs are picked at random (fixed-seed xorshift, so runs are deterministic) until the payment and fee are covered, then random extras are added while they move the selected total closer to 2x the payment (never past 3x). Change is shaped like the payment: up to one change output per payment output, sized like it, with the remainder in the last. If random selection cannot cover the payment (or the transaction would be too large) it falls back to largest-first; it refuses only when the whole wallet cannot pay. JSON is parsed and written by hand for exactly the protocol's messages.
submissions.summary: CIP-2 random-improve in Rust: random selection until covered, improvement towards 2x the payment, change shaped like the payment outputs, largest-first fallback.
random-improve plus opportunistic consolidation: also spends up to 3 of the smallest UTxOs under 2 ADA when the extra fee is below their value, to reduce dust.

submit_steps: Pick an <id> (lowercase a-z, 0-9, -). Put submission.toml and an executable build.sh in the directory, plus whatever your code needs. A whole codebase is fine, under max_bytes (4 MiB) in challenge.toml. build.sh runs offline in a sandbox, must leave an executable ./select in the directory (see contracts/wallet/INTERFACE.md), and must vendor any dependencies.

submission.toml declares: id (the dir name), contract = "wallet@1", novelty, direction, parent, taxonomy (keys strategy, change, consolidation, language; see taxonomy.toml), summary, optional claims (for the declared property change-privacy only) and model.

Novelty is your own declaration and is never judged. new starts a direction <name> that no accepted submission uses. builds-on names an accepted parent; copy its directory and edit it. The direction is inherited. A port to another language, or a new name, seed or constant on an accepted approach, is builds-on, not new.
Run the judge locally first (see README.md). CI then builds your submission and runs the same judge, which checks the properties and measures every axis. Those numbers are a claim from the PR run.

There is no record to beat and no minimum improvement. If the checks pass, the PR is landed on main automatically, two clean runs there record it on the map, and the PR is closed. Failing and noisy attempts are recorded too.
challenges.summary: Cardano wallets must choose which UTxOs to spend for each payment (CIP-2). The transaction pays a fee that grows with its size, so fewer inputs is cheaper now. But always spending the biggest coins leaves a wallet full of small leftovers (dust) that cost more to spend later, and spending many small ones now costs fees today. Cheap online heuristics answer fast; exact searches find tidier selections but take longer. There is no single winner, which is what the map on the site is for.

axes.definition: How inputs are chosen for a payment

values.definition: Sort by value, take the biggest UTxOs until the payment and fee are covered
CIP-2 random-improve: pick UTxOs at random, then improve towards an ideal change size
Depth-first search with pruning for a selection with no or minimal change
Dynamic-programming or heuristic subset-sum over the UTxO values
Tries every subset (only practical for small wallets or with a cut-off)
Anything else; name it in the summary

axes.definition: What happens to the leftover value after paying

values.definition: Several change outputs, to keep the wallet granular
Change sized like the payment, so it is hard to tell from it
Searches for an input set that needs no change, else falls back

axes.definition: Whether the wallet merges small UTxOs while paying

values.definition: Never adds inputs only to merge dust
Adds small inputs when they are cheap to carry
Consolidates once the wallet holds more than a chosen number of UTxOs

axes.definition: What the submission is written in

rules.reason: Largest-first stops at the first coins that cover the payment, so it seldom lands on an amount that needs no change; finding one means searching subsets
rules.text: change = none-when-possible needs an exact-match search (branch-and-bound or exhaustive), not largest-first

rules.reason: Each extra input adds 140 bytes to the transaction, 6,160 lovelace of fee at min_fee_a = 44
rules.text: consolidation other than none costs extra inputs per transaction: expect it to trade fees now for dust later

challenges.prompt:
You are helping me contribute to the ledger-cbor challenge: make cardano-ledger decode real mainnet Conway transactions in fewer CPU instructions, without changing what it decodes or what it rejects. This is the decoder cardano-node runs on every transaction, so a decoder that accepts or rejects anything differently is a consensus bug, not a speedup. Correctness comes first: a faster decoder that differs from the reference anywhere is rejected.

Setup
- The challenge lives in the private repo github.com/Ryun1/auto-research-challenge-builder, under challenges/ledger-cbor/. I am a collaborator on it. If it is not cloned yet: git clone git@github.com:Ryun1/auto-research-challenge-builder.git
- Before changing anything, read challenges/ledger-cbor/README.md (goal, scoring, policy) and challenges/ledger-cbor/SUBMITTING.md (the full walkthrough). They are the source of truth. If this prompt and those files disagree, follow the files and tell me.
- Start from the latest main: git fetch origin && git switch -c <my-github-name>/ledger-cbor-<idea> origin/main
- Push branches to this repo. Do not fork: a pull request from a fork gets no score comment.

How it is scored
- The score is speedup = reference instructions / candidate instructions, counted by Callgrind on a fresh sample of recent mainnet transactions that CI draws after the code is built. A paired wall-time check rejects a change that makes decoding measurably slower.
- A change counts only if it beats the current record by at least 1%. The record and every earlier attempt are in challenges/ledger-cbor/results.jsonl: read it to see where the bar is and what has been tried.
- Correct means identical to the reference on every input: the same decoded value, the same re-encoded bytes, the same accept or reject decision on mutated inputs, and nothing left unevaluated that the reference evaluates.

What you may change
- Only existing .hs files under challenges/ledger-cbor/candidate/<package>/src/. No new, deleted or renamed files, and nothing outside candidate/.
- No new unsafe* functions, FFI, Template Haskell, CPP lines, IO or imports of GHC internals. The Policy section of the README has the exact allowlist. Everything under candidate/ must stay below 4 MiB in total.

Where to look
- A profile of the reference shows the editable packages running about a quarter of the instructions directly (mary 9%, binary 6%, babbage, conway and alonzo 5%, core 3%) and the GHC runtime another 38%, much of it closure application and allocation that the shape of the decoders decides. A Rust decoder (pallas) needs about 4.5x fewer instructions on the same transactions, so there is room.
- One change that scored about 1% as a pull request replaced a decode that went through the Coders interpreter (the MaryValue pair) with a direct decoder. Similar places are worth checking, but treat that as a lead, not a finding: measure.
- Keep error behaviour and laziness exactly as they are.

How to work
1. Pick one idea, small enough to reason about. One idea per pull request.
2. Make the change, then run the gate. It works on macOS and Linux and needs only git and Rust:
   cargo build --release && ./target/release/cb gate --base origin/main --head HEAD
   It must print "gate ok: ledger-cbor".
3. If this machine is Linux with GHC 9.6.7, cabal 3.16 and valgrind, build and measure locally from challenges/ledger-cbor/: ./setup.sh (35+ minutes the first time), then ./build.sh, CB_SEED=1 ./verifier/run and CB_SEED=1 ./bench/run. The build does not work on macOS: skip this step there and let CI build it.
4. Commit, push the branch and open a pull request against main. In the description say what changed, why the decoder still accepts, rejects and evaluates exactly what it did before, and any numbers you measured.
5. CI comments the result on the pull request, usually within tens of minutes. Read it and tell me the status and the speedup. "valid claim better" means it beats the record by 1% and is ready for the maintainer. "rejected" with "verify failed" means the output differs from the reference somewhere.

Limits
- Do not push to main and do not merge the pull request. The maintainer merges, and two fresh runs on main then decide whether it becomes the record.
- Do not edit the judge, the tests, the workflows or results.jsonl.
- Report honestly. Local numbers come from a public sample and are only a guide; the score is CI's. If an idea does not pay off, say so and show the numbers instead of tuning until it looks good.
- Every push to a pull request costs the organisers build time, and the pipeline refuses an account's pushes after 10 in 24 hours. Measure before you push, and ask me before starting a second idea.
submit_steps: Branch, don't fork. You are a collaborator, so push a branch to this repo and open the PR from it against main.

Build and test locally (Linux only). The build needs GHC 9.6.7, cabal 3.16, python3, rsync and the Cardano system libraries (libsodium, secp256k1, blst). Scoring also needs valgrind. setup.sh uses GNU sed -i, so it fails on macOS. On a Mac, edit there and build on a Linux machine, or let CI build it.
Open the PR and read the result. Opening the PR, and every later push to it, starts the Submission workflow. A new push cancels the run in progress for that PR.

After the merge. The maintainer merges PRs one at a time. The merge starts the Promote workflow on main, which takes about 20 minutes with warm caches (longer after a cold rebuild). It makes two independent runs, each on its own fresh pool and seed. challenges.summary: Make cardano-ledger decode real mainnet Conway transactions in fewer instructions, without changing what it decodes or what it rejects. The editable code is the src/ of the decoding stack: cardano-ledger-binary (the Decoder monad, Annotator, coders, primitives), cardano-ledger-core and the era packages from Shelley to Conway (the per-field instances, MaryValue, BabbageTxOut, the Conway tx body...).
